prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which thousands of atoms are held in a magic-wavelength lattice and interrogated free of Doppler, recoil and first-order light shifts, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B002 to B022, and I want to say why in scientific terms rather than because the support count favours it. My first-round criterion was that the prize should reward a clue from nature, not an elegant instrument. The lattice clock does not meet that in the strictest sense, since limits on drifting constants and dark matter are still limits. But my colleagues convinced me that this criterion was too narrow as I applied it. The Academy's own wording is discovery or invention, and the magic-wavelength lattice is a sharply defined invention with physics content: it was not obvious that thousands of atoms could be interrogated with no first-order light shift or motional broadening, and the result is that systematic effects, not the atoms, set the limit. Independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) reach about 1e-18 and agree when compared directly, which is exactly the independent reproduction I ask of any result, and millimetre-scale gravitational redshift is already a measurement of nature that was out of reach before. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the concept and the first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking it to the accuracy and stability frontier. The redefinition of the second belongs to metrology, and the scientific recognition does not need to wait for it. For the citation I would answer the chair's first question directly: the unit is the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice, which is distinct from the comb (a ruler, 2005) and from single-ion control (one absorber, 2012), and the citation should say so.
statement.case_against: My remaining reservation is the one I raised in round 1: this is a superb measurement advance that so far gives us limits rather than a surprise from nature, and it sits in a lineage honoured in 2005 and 2012. I now regard that as a matter of emphasis rather than a bar, but I would not want the citation to over-claim fundamental discoveries that have not been made. Credit is also not complete: Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Ovsiannikov and others contributed to the early strontium work and cannot be named within two. Separately, I am giving up B002 not because the science is weaker but because the credit problem I conceded is real. Two survey collaborations of hundreds made the 2005 detections, the theory of the acoustic peak lies with Peebles and Yu and with Sunyaev and Zeldovich, and a trio of Eisenstein, Cole and Peacock is a choice among many. A third cosmology prize after 2006, 2011 and 2019 is a further cost.

responses.point: Olsson argues that the lattice clock is a discovery-and-invention case, with Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength concept realised in strontium and Ye's group delivering 1e-18, and she has a serious difficulty with a three-name BAO attribution.
responses.response: You are right about BAO, and I should have weighed it more heavily in round 1. Three names cannot represent two survey collaborations plus the theoretical predecessors, and you say plainly that we might not be crediting the people who did the work. I accept that and it is the main reason I have moved. On the clock, I agree that Katori's concept and Ye's performance are separable contributions, but your own caution about Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and Lemonde stands. I would ask that the committee's expert review check the 2005 to 2008 strontium lattice papers before the final ballot, so that the citation does not claim priority the record does not support.

responses.point: Pearce, as Chair, argues that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb (a ruler) and the 2012 single-ion prize (one absorber) because many atoms are interrogated at once, and that this should be in the citation. He keeps BAO as a future candidate and has moved from IceCube.
responses.response: Your ruler versus one absorber versus many atoms distinction is the clearest answer to the overlap worry and I have adopted it in my citation text. I also accept your reply to my discovery-versus-instrument objection: discovery or invention is the Academy's own formulation, and a technique that moves a limit by two orders of magnitude and opens new tests meets it. I still consider IceCube a real discovery from nature and I ranked it fourth, but Kroll's question about separating Halzen's and Karle's roles from a collaboration of about 300 stays open, and I agree that independent confirmation from a second detector is thinner than for the clock. I am glad to see BAO kept as a candidate for a later year.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the clock is the cleanest credit on the shortlist, that Takamoto's 2005 demonstration is largely covered by Katori's name, and that the 2005 and 2012 exposure cannot be used against only one candidate.
responses.response: I accept your point that the same exposure to 2005 and 2012 applies to trapped ions, and so it is not a fair argument against B022 alone. On Takamoto I am less sure than you that Katori's name covers everything: he was Katori's group member, so that is reasonable, but Lemonde's group and Ye's own early strontium papers appeared in parallel and I would like the documentation to confirm Katori's priority rather than assume it. I note your conflict disclosure about Hall and JILA. I think it is correctly stated, and I do not see it as requiring recusal, because proximity to a laureate's former environment is not a tie to either credited person.

responses.point: Mehlig describes the lattice clock as an application of known atomic physics and would put the conceptual novelty of a classifying invariant above a smaller uncertainty budget, while naming B022 as his first alternative and noting that B022 is the safer prize if uncontested allocation is weighted highest.
responses.response: I share your taste for a result that classifies matter, and that is why I rank B045 as an alternative. But I do not think the argument that magic-wavelength trapping is an application of known atomic physics is fair. The idea of choosing a wavelength where both clock levels shift equally, in a lattice that confines atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, was not a standard step, and its payoff is the ability to use thousands of atoms. For topological insulators I would add the credit problem of the BHZ proposal, with Zhang deceased, to your own concern about 2016. If the committee cannot settle that with documents, I think your fallback to B022 is the right one.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first but argues that the 2016 prize covered a different discovery, and says he would sooner see B022 awarded cleanly than force a contested three-name list.
responses.response: I accept your correction on 2016. That prize honoured topological phase transitions and Haldane's work, and the helical edge states of Z2 insulators are a separate discovery. I withdraw my suggestion that it is a serious overlap. My difficulty remains the credit: omitting the BHZ proposal that Molenkamp tested, and the 3D case, is a real problem for a trio, and I cannot see how the committee resolves it without documentation. If the committee wants a topological prize, Kane, Mele and Molenkamp with a quantum spin Hall citation is the most defensible version, but I would then keep B045 as my alternative rather than my choice.

uncertainties: Whether the committee's expert review confirms Katori's priority for the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock against the parallel work of Ye, Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and Hinkley.
Whether the 1e-18 agreement between independent laboratories is documented well enough in direct comparisons, not just in separately reported uncertainty budgets.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the redefinition of the second; I think it need not, but I accept that others weigh practical impact differently.
Whether BAO could in a later year be given a defensible credit structure, and whether DESI evolving dark-energy results will firm up by then.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any credited name on B022, B002 or B045. My research on dark energy and de Sitter space is in the same broad area as BAO, which affects scientific interest but implies no personal or institutional tie, and David Gross, my PhD supervisor, is not among the candidates. I have noted Johansson's declared interest in B039 and B032 and Kroll's proximity to the JILA environment. I regard neither as affecting B022 requiring recusal. As Secretary I would also want expert reports on Katori and Ye's priority before the final ballot.
